The report was presented by Piedmont Police Chief Jeremy Bowers. The PPD Annual Report showed a significant reduction in property crimes in 2024, primarily larceny. articles.text: The City of Piedmont is inviting community members to provide input on standards for new housing in Piedmont at their Objective Design Standards Open House on Wednesday, February 12, from 6:00-8:00 p.m. at Piedmont Community Hall. At the event, residents will have an opportunity to learn what objective design standards are, speak directly with the project team, and share their preferences and priorities for what should be included in standards in Piedmont. After a brief presentation (delivered twice during the event), attendees will dive deeper into the project at a series of staffed displays and share feedback on questions like: • What they like most about the built environment in Piedmont today • What types of site design elements would make new housing feel compatible with existing neighborhoods • What design elements they feel are most important to be included in objective standards State law now requires cities to approve certain new housing proposals, including accessory dwelling units and SB9 applications, based on “objective” standards – those that require no subject judgement or interpretation by public officials. rules for elements like articulation, type of design, and massing, the City can provide residents, property owners, and developers clear and consistent expectations for what new housing in Piedmont will look like. This helps streamline the development process and removes barriers to new housing. In Piedmont, objective design standards already exist for accessory dwelling units (ADUs) and multi-family and mixed-use developments. This initiative will develop new objective standards for one-to four-unit residential development and update the existing standards for other housing types. A video introduction to Objective Design Standards is available at piedmont.ca.gov/ODSBasics. For more information, visit the project website at piedmont. ca.gov/ODS. City seeks community input on residential design standards The City of Piedmont is inviting community members to provide input on standards for new housing in Piedmont at their Objective Design Standards Open House on Wednesday, February 12, from 6:00-8:00 p.m. at Piedmont Community Hall. At the event, residents will have an opportunity to learn what objective design standards are, speak directly with the project team, and share their preferences and priorities for what should be included in standards in Piedmont. After a brief presentation (delivered twice during the event), attendees will dive deeper into the project at a series of staffed displays and share feedback on questions like: • What they like most about the built environment in Piedmont today • What types of site design elements would make new housing feel compatible with existing neighborhoods • What design elements they feel are most important to be included in objective standards State law now requires cities to approve certain new housing proposals, including accessory dwelling units and SB9 applications, based on “objective” standards – those that require no subject judgement or interpretation by public officials. By adopting clearly defined rules for elements like articulation, type of design, and massing, the City can provide residents, property owners, and developers clear and consistent expectations for what new housing in Piedmont will look like. This helps streamline the development process and removes barriers to new housing. In Piedmont, objective design standards already exist for accessory dwelling units (ADUs) and multi-family and mixed-use developments. This initiative will develop new objective standards for one-to four-unit residential development and update the existing standards for other housing types. articles.text: Piedmont City Council voted on January 21 to award a contract to Rapid Grading Services for a project that involves repaving the length of Grand Avenue in Piedmont, adding bulb-outs and installing green infrastructure. The contract was approved for an amount of $1,414,102 with a construction budget of $1,555,513. A significant portion of the funding – $500,000 of it – is coming from an Alameda County Transportation Commission grant that the City applied for in the summer of 2002. Key elements of the project include a two-inch grind and resurfacing of the pavement, installation of ADA compliant curb ramps and bulb-outs, bicycle markings, and a bioretention basin that provides soil-filtering of storm water. Additionally, this pavement rehabilitation project would meet all of the Green Infrastructure needs that are required under the City’s municipal permit, satisfying Alameda County requirements. The soil-filtering areas of the project will be furnished with drought-resistant plants such as salvia, sea lavender, California gray flush, and coyote mint. When asked by City Council about the effectiveness of the proposed bulb-outs, Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales cited observations of traffic officers that vehicles moved slower after their installation. Although there were no statistics cited, Gonzales offered to come back with more data if requested. “Narrowing a roadway is the single most effective tool that is recommended for traffic calming, and so this design is very much consistent with that,” said Gonzales. The bid documents allow for 90 working days, or 18 weeks, of construction time. Not including possible delays from weather, the City estimates construction should be completed this summer. articles.text: In an effort to stay on top of federal telecommunications law, Piedmont City Council voted to approve the first reading of an ordinance that amends design standards for wireless communications facilities (WCFs) at its meeting on Monday, February 3. WCF is an encompassing term for equipment and structures that broadcast and receive wireless frequencies such as antennas, connection cables, broadband equipment or wireless tower structures. After a series of study sessions with the Planning Commission and City Council, City Staff developed a set of proposed standards with the aim to strike a balance between the need for modern wireless infrastructure and the preservation of Piedmont’s landscape setting and building standards. Piedmont’s Planning Department outlined three key goals to guide the new standards: minimize visual impact, enhance wireless coverage, and comply with applicable laws. The standards highly encourage “stealth” designs which conceal wireless equipment to appear as an everyday feature. The presentation showed examples of concealed designs in Piedmont such as equipment integrated into lamp posts, hidden in building towers, or disguised as chimneys. Revised standards include updated height limits, strengthened visual impact mitigation, incorporated city standards for right-of-way facilities, and establishment of a 10-year permit term. Residents may review the new standards in the agenda report for the January 13, 2025 Planning Commission Meeting. A list of meeting agendas and recordings can be found on the City’s Live Content and Video Archive at https://piedmont.ca.gov/news/ kcom-t v/live_content_and _ video_archive.

articles.text: As standardized testing continues to evolve, many families wonder how AP exams, which take place each May, fit into their student’s college roadmap. We want to help sift through the enormity of information available on the internet, and provide insight into some of the questions we are most frequently asked… • Do AP exams matter for college admissions? The short answer is yes! AP exams can be impactful for college admissions. Depending on exam scores, students may be eligible for specific merit scholarships or receive college credit. AP exams allow schools to evaluate a student’s readiness for the rigor of college courses. • My student signed up for an AP exam back in October; must they take the test? They do not have to take the test, but, unless there is an extenuating circumstance, most students should. If the test goes well, they have a great quantitative addition to their apps. • My student is doing well in their AP class; will they do well on the AP exam? This is a tricky one! AP classes are not standardized like the exam; there is often great variety in rigor, grading, and expectations. The best way to know how a student will do on an AP exam is by taking a practice test. • If my student’s AP class isn’t preparing them for the exam, what can they do? All students who are enrolled in an AP course have access to “AP classroom”. This is a great resource for official practice problems and course content. If a student wants more individualized support, they can always talk to their teacher or engage a tutor. • What changes are coming to the AP exams this year? Starting this May, there will be 16 fully digital exams – African American Studies, Art History, Comparative Government and Politics, Computer Science A and Principles, English Language and Literature, Environmental Science, European History, Human Geography, Latin, Psychology, Seminar, United States Government and Politics, United States History and World History: Modern; and 12 hybrid exams – Biology, Calculus AB and BC, Chemistry, Macro and Microeconomics, Physics (1, 2, and C), Precalculus, and Statistics. While AP classes and exams can be an important factor in college admissions, their true intent is to help students gain important knowledge and skills that will help them succeed in college and beyond. Study Smarter has been providing individualized academic tutoring, test preparation, and college counseling to Piedmont families since 1997. articles.text: The East Bay Hills FIRST Tech Challenge (FTC) League celebrated its first season with a tournament held at Piedmont Middle School on Sunday, January 26. The event showcased the ingenuity and dedication of 16 teams from across the region (including 8 from Piedmont), highlighting the remarkable talent in youth robotics. Tournament Highlights: • Champion: Circuit Breakers (Team 21419) from Piedmont, CA, emerged as the tournament champion, demonstrating exceptional engineering and strategy throughout the competition. Serving as the captain of the winning alliance, they have secured advancement to the regional tour nament. Throughout the league meets, the Circuit Breakers maintained an impressive record, achieving 10 wins and zero losses. They maintained their unbeaten streak throughout the tournament, winning all 5 of their qualification matches and each of their three playoff showdowns. • Finalist: Piedmont Pioneers (Team 11201) from Piedmont, CA, secured the finalist position, showcasing impressive performance and teamwork. • Inspire Award: The Patriots (Team 3470) from Brentwood, CA, were honored with the Inspire Award for embodying the ‘challenge’ of the FTC program and serving as a role model for other teams. As winners of this award, the Patriots will also advance to the regional tournament. This season’s events included three league meets leading up to the league tournament, each providing teams with opportunities to refine their robots and strategies. articles.text: Troop 15 In January Piedmont Scouts in Troop 15 had an excellent trip to Pinnacles National Park, near Soledad, for a weekend of hiking and car camping. Everybody started with their packs and a healthy dose of energy; then drove two and a half hours to the park. We dropped our packs off at the campsite and brought our daypacks and lunches to the shuttle that took us to the trailhead. Due to the limited shuttle capacity and long shuttle wait time, we split into two groups. Thirty waited for the buses, and 14 of us decided to make the 3-mile walk to the trailhead. But our decision was in vain. Instead of taking the regular schedule, two buses came only five minutes after the first, with ample space for the whole troop. Troop 15 Scouts Leo Thakur and Abbie Gregovich are getting ready to prepare burgers for dinner. Rainbow viewed in the sky at Pinnacles Troop 15 Scouts hiking the trail to the High Peak at Pinnacles We didn’t know that as we walked the additional three miles with a cheerful demeanor. One older Scout brought a frisbee that we used to pass the time. Our group tossed the frisbee 214 consecutive times. The gravel path followed a riverbed, eventually leading into a canyon filled with moss-covered boulders. After an hour, we made it to the most exciting part of Pinnacles – the caves. The Bear Gulch caves we traversed were created when massive boulders eroded and fell from the adjacent rock face onto extremely narrow crevices. Because of this formation the beginning of the cave felt like we were walking between large stones, not an enclosed space. As we went further, the environment chilled, and we hit a pitch-black chamber with a roughly carved staircase. Equipped with our flashlights and jumping between pockets of light, we took photos at every turn. The top section of the lower cavern captivated us the most, because, from that height, we could see the deep pools formed over millions of years on either side. articles.text: League title fight tonight at Bishop O’Dowd Staff Photos Piedmont’s girls’ basketball team picked up three easy wins last week and squares up for a WACC Foothill title-fight against Bishop O’Dowd tonight. Piedmont High’s girls’ basketball team got the job done with three expected wins last week. They beat Castro Valley 73-28 on the road on Wednesday, January 29, handled San Leandro a 61-20 pounding in the Pirates’ new gym on Friday, January 31, and then obliterated Weston Ranch 54-12 the following day at Binks Rawlings Gym. Their record improved to 17-4 overall and 4-1 in league. It all builds to the most important game of the regular season for the Highlanders tonight, squaring up against Western Alameda County Conference leaders, Bishop O’Dowd tonight in the Dragons’ home gym. Piedmont needs to win its remaining league games to split the WACC Foothill title with O’Dowd after dropping their first meeting 56-47 back on January 14. “The biggest thing is to just play the way we’ve been playing and lock in for all four quarters,” said coach Bryan Gardere. ”In each of our losses, we’ve fallen behind in the late third quarter or fourth quarter. Everyone got experience in that first O’Dowd game, now they know what to expect.” Last year, Piedmont won Savannah Dennig had a double-double against San Leandro. the opening meeting against the Dragons but lost the second game, settling for a shared WACC title with O’Dowd. Senior Shakila Zuberi has been a varsity member all four years of her high school career, while her eight other teammates are in the midst of their first year at PHS. Zuberi knows about the intensity this game brings. “We’re taking in our desire and how much we want it. Now that we’ve felt that defeat, we don’t want it to happen again. I want to see us recognize who scores for O’Dowd, how they score, and to take those points away,” Zuberi said. Although it’s a big game with a league title on the line, Dennig cautions against psyching themselves out. “We’ve learned to treat it as another game, we’re going to play hard the whole game and be aggressive. I’ve learned a lot of people treat it much larger than the typical high school game, but we just need to treat it with the same intensity as these other games,” added freshman Savannah Dennig. 73-28 win over Castro Valley Piedmont led 14-5 through the first quarter and jumped out to a 35-15 lead by halftime. PHS extended the gap to 53-24 by the start of the fourth quarter, adding 20 more points in the final going while only allowing four. Final stats: Jenelle Solis led with 21 points, three rebounds, six assists, and a steal. Briana Webb had 13 points, six rebounds, and four steals. Taylor White had nine points, 16 rebounds, eight assists, and two steals. Dennig Shakila Zuberi is a senior on the girls’ basketball team.

articles.text: Lose 50-49 to Castro Valley in another league thriller It’s been a week of drama for Piedmont’s boys’ basketball team, which split results in two league games, each by one point. The Highlanders recently spoiled the party for San Leandro in the Pirates’ brand new $60 million gym on January 31, winning 61-60 with the a go-ahead basket with 25 seconds left. Two days earlier they lost 50-49 to Castro Valley in the Trojans’ gym. Piedmont has proven to be a gritty team when their backs are against the wall, outscoring San Leandro in both the third and fourth quarters. “It was nice to get this win after the loss to Castro Valley, especially when we’re down a few starters. We shot the ball extremely well despite not being super crisp; the heart was there, the energy was there,” coach Ben Spencer said. “It was almost the same situation against Castro Valley. We took the loss against CV, so we were hungry this time. We played great defense, got steals, and knocked down free throws in the clutch,” said senior captain Ravi Silverberg. Silverberg hit the go-ahead score late in the fourth to put PHS up 59-58. Finishing with 19 points, Silverberg and teammates had to do it without their leading scorer, Dillon Casey, who suffered an injury early in the fourth quarter. Starting forward P.J. Brayer also missed the game. “We were down a bunch of starters and then Dillon goes down. I never felt like the day was lost. Everyone was ready to play—from the last guy off of the bench to the first guys on the court,” Silverberg said. It was a big moment for sophomore Beach Lorin, a new starter on the varsity roster. He nabbed a steal at midcourt after Silververg’s basket, drew a foul and converted two critical free throws for a 61-58 lead. It proved to be especially important when SL scored a field goal as time expired. “It was exciting, I saw the pass and just went for it. To know we had the lead and got the ball, it felt great,” Lorin said. 61-60 over San Leandro Piedmont and San Leandro were tied 14-14 through the first quarter and trailed 32-30 at halftime. The Pirates came out hot Staff Photos The moment Ravi Silverberg scored the go-ahead basket against San Leandro’s best player with about 25 seconds left. Beach Lorin with his big steal at the end of the game to help solidify the win over San Leandro.

articles.text: 2 goals wiped in 1-0 loss to Berkeley with poor officiating Piedmont’s girls’ soccer team walked out of last week with a win and a loss in two road games against Western Alameda County Conference foes. They beat Encinal 2-0 at Estuary Park in Alameda on Wednesday, January 29 but lost 1-0 to Berkeley two days later on a cold and rainy night, and a game marred by poor officiating. Piedmont waswithout four key players: midfield captain Louisa Symkowick, Kyla Williams, Kyra Trombi, and Chloe Toyoma. Compounding the problem, leading scorer Elsa Wallway suffered an injury in the first half and could not return. The pair of results brings Piedmont’s record to 5-2-7 (W-TL) and 2-1-4 against league competition. Piedmont has just three games left in its regular season as they vie for a North Coast Section berth. They visit Castro Valley tonight, February 5, travel to Bishop O’Dowd on February 11, and play the season-final hosting Encinal on February 13. 2-0 over Encinal Piedmont first offensive action came in the ninth minute when freshman Kyla Williams stole possession of an Encinal defender, dribbling into the box before taking a shot on target. They had another chance in the 11th when Eliza Hammond was the target on a near-post run from a corner, but her shot went wide. Williams had another shot trail high in the 28th and one on target two minutes later to force a diving save. Ryo Woltag had a shot go narrowly wide in the 37th minute. Piedmont finally broke through in the 39th when Ava Sauer sent a long pass to Hannah Sullivan—who redirected it out of the air and toward net. Encinal’s keeper botched the grab, allowing it slowly roll in. Juliana Thornborrow had a goal against Encinal. Staff Photos In the second half, Woltag had another shot go wide in the 60th minute. Piedmont got its second goal in the 70th when Williams played a slick through pass to Juliana Thornborrow making a run behind the Jets’ back line. Thornborrow pushed it around the approaching keeper in close distance to roll her shot into the net. Loss to Berkeley Despite Berkeley claiming a clean sheet, Piedmont still had its chances. Wallway had a shot on target that the keeper fumbled in the fourth minute, while Piedmont wanted a hand-ball called on Berkeley seconds later but it wasn’t given. Woltag also had a shot go narrowly high in the sixth. Berkeley capitalized on a pass out of the back straight to a Yellowjackets’ forward, launching a shot from atop the penalty area for the game’s only goal in the 10th minute. After that Wallway had a shot go high in the 13th and the two sides traded possession until halftime. Wallway suffered a game-ending injury after taking a hard fall in the final minutes of the first half. Piedmont had a good scoring chance in the 55th when a pass from a corner bobbled around in the penalty area, leading to a shot on target by Stephanie Lee that was cleared off of the line. The Highlanders contended the ball went across the line, but wasn’t awarded the goal. The Highlanders were harddone yet again in the 75th when the sideline judge wiped away a Piedmont goal. In the buildup, Samantha Ronen retrieved a failed clearance by a Berkeley defender, feeding it to Hannah Sullivan in front of the net for the goal. However, the sideline ref called Sullivan offside despite Ronen being the highest up the field with a defender tailing close by. NEXT UP Piedmont (5-2-7 overall, 2-1-4 league) travels to Castro Valley tonight, February 5, at 6:00 p.m. They also visit Bishop O’Dowd in Oakland on Tuesday, February 11 at 6:30 p.m. Hannah Sullivan scored once against Encinal. Kyla Williams had a slick assist to Juliana Thonborrow in their win over the Jets.

articles.text: Staff Photos Harper Mand (35) celebrates his goal against Hayward. Also pictured is Gianluca Bini (left) and Callum Long. The Highlanders answered a two-game skid to get back in the win column on Thursday, January 30, beating the visiting Hayward Farmers by a 3-1 score. Two days earlier, Piedmont lost a high-scoring 3-2 to match to Mt. Eden, also at Witter Field. The pair of results brings PHS’ record to 5-3-7 (W-TL) and 3-2-3 in league. “I’m happy for the boys to finally get a result. I was pleased to see some concepts we’re looking for. We talk about playing conscious and subconscious thinking; we were very conscious in the first 10 minutes and then you see fatigue, then bad habits kick in,” said coach Ben Russell. Piedmont has proven to be its most productive during set pieces so far this season with four goals on set pieces in the last three games. Two of their goals against Hayward came by way of passes from free kicks; they scored one from a corner against Mt. Eden, while their score in a 3-1 loss to Bishop O’Dowd on January 24 was from a lofted ball by Roman Ahearn. “Set pieces have been something we’ve worked on since the start of the season, it’s a good foundation for us. It’s something the boys have taken to. We have a lot of height on the team; it’s just turning it into more games. I think the chance creation is there,” Russell said. The center back pairing of Elias Reed-Miguel and Max Goldfarb produced assists on goals on free kicks against Hayward. “We have a lot of height with our attackers. We know if we can get the ball into the box, then we can create goals pretty easily. It’s great to get results in games like this so we can build confidence for the harder teams,” Reed-Miguel said. Piedmont has just three matches against tough competition to close its season as they look to solidify a North Coast Section playoff berth. They visit clinched league champions Berkeley on February 7, host Bishop O’Dowd on February 11, and close the season at Castro Valley on February 13. 3-1 win over Hayward Piedmont goal keeper Lucas Malecki started the game with a huge save in close distance in the fourth minute. Three minutes later, Goldfarb sent a pass from a free kick to Gianluca Bini for a header on target, but it was saved. Bini was the target of a corner in the ninth, but his header was off of the mark. PHS broke the deadlock in the 20th minute when Niko Markopoulos fired a hard shot that forced a diving save, rebounding to Jacques Saldanha in front to slot it in. It took just two more minutes for Piedmont to score when Reed-Miguel launched a free kick from the left sideline to freshman Jimmy Lagios at the far post for a header goal. Hayward scored by way of a corner in the 24th while Piedmont went into halftime with a 2-1 lead. Piedmont’s next goal came in the 65th when Goldfarb whipped in a low cross from a free kick on the right sideline into the box, meeting Harper Mand, whose shot looped off of a defender. 3-2 victory over Mt. Eden Piedmont scored quickly in the second minute after drawing a corner. Ahearn sent a cross in a cross targeting Bini, who headed a ball centrally to Mand, volleying it out of the air into the net. Bosco Lorin almost scored in Elias Reed-Miguel had one of Piedmont’s two assists from free kicks.

articles.text: The first U.S. solo exhibition of work by Amol K Patil, a visual artist whose work explores issues of class and caste in his native Mumbai, India, will be on view at Berkeley Art Museum now through April 27. “MATRIX 286 / Amol K Patil: A Forest of Remembrance” will feature paintings and sculptures by Patil, all newly commissioned for the BAMPFA presentation. The exhibition marks the latest installment in BAMPFA’s signature contemporary art exhibition series “MATRIX,” an experimental platform for artists to make and show new work. Over the past decade, Patil has established himself as a premier voice in India’s contemporary art scene through a multidisciplinary practice that includes painting, sculpture, video installation and live performance. In both abstract and figurative forms, Patil illuminates the experience of marginalized communities in India’s highly stratified urban settings, where poverty and caste discrimination have led to massive levels of inequality. Patil’s work often references Mumbai’s chawls — the century-old social housing originally built for mill workers and other laborers, where the city’s working classes have since managed to create vibrant shared living spaces against a backdrop of economic precarity. In Patil’s BAMPFA-commissioned series of painting and sculptures, the chawl is reimagined as a space of historical memory and present resistance, highlighting the resilience of the multigenerational families who persevere there. Working with cast bronze sculpture, Patil has crafted a series of five figurative sculptures that obliquely reference the tangled bodies and cramped living conditions of chawl households — where families often live in units as small as 120 square feet. These sculptures will appear alongside a new series of 19 paintings that expressionistically render everyday life in the The first U.S. solo exhibition of work by Amol K Patil will be on view at Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Fine Arts now through April 27. chawls, drawing on the personal and communal histories of these sites. “We are thrilled to present this newly commissioned body of work by Amol K Patil for his first U.S. solo exhibition,” said BAMPFA’s Chief Curator Margot Norton. “Patil’s poetic and deeply moving sculptures and paintings bring the everyday experiences of those living in India’s chawls into vibrant relief, depicting intimate moments to reveal urgent societal concerns.” Patil is a conceptual and performance artist based in Mumbai. Following his education in the visual arts from Rachana Sansad Academy of Fine Arts and Crafts, Mumbai, he has made work that explores the intersection of performance art, theater, music, kinetic art, and video installation. He was a 2022-2024 resident at the Rijksakademie in Amsterdam. In 2023, he received his first international solo exhibition at the Hayward Gallery in London. Patil’s grandfather was a noted interpreter and poet, and his father was an avant-garde playwright. Berkeley Art Museum is located a 2155 Center Street and is open 11 a.m. through 7 p.m., Wednesday through Sunday. Tickets ($18 general admission) and more details are available at bampfa.org. articles.text: This Saturday, February 8 through March 9, see the Northern California premiere of 2023 Pulitzer Prize finalist Lloyd Suh’s The Heart Sellers at Aurora Theatre in Berkeley. The humorous and heartwarming play about the Asian immigrant experience offers a personal portrait of the impact of the landmark 1965 Hart-Celler Act that revoked certain barriers to immigration and citizenship in favor of a skills-based preference system. Set in 1973 during the aftermath of Watergate, The Heart Sellers centers on two Asian women navigating their first American Thanksgiving. Starting out as strangers who meet in the grocery store, Luna (Nicole Javier) from the Philippines and Jane (Wonjung Kim) from South Korea find common ground in their shared experiences of often absent medical resident husbands, missing families and friends back home and discovering the joys and challenges of life in America. As the women attempt to cook Thanksgiving dinner for the first time, they dream of discotheques, Disneyland and the future. Acclaimed director, actor and playwright Jennifer Chang, who directed the World Premiere of the show at Milwaukee Repertory Theater, will co-direct the show Aurora Theatre in Berkeley is presenting The Heart Sellers, an acclaimed new play being shown February 8 through March 9. Pictured are Nicole Javier and Wonjung Kim in the lead roles as Luna and Jane. with Lloyd Suh. “I have long been a fan of Suh’s work and ‘The Heart Sellers’ is the epitome of everything we aspire to present on our stages,” said TheatreWorks Artistic Director Giovanna Sardelli. “It’s so funny and filled with heart. Pinpointing the personal during a pivotal moment in our history, this uplifting play offers a moving tribute to those who make America their home. This is a beautiful story that needs to be told.” The New York Times called the play “beautiful” and “politically astute.” “My first thought after I read this play was that we must produce it,” said Michael Stevenson, Artistic Director of production company Capital Stage. “The beautiful story of these women’s friendship made me fall in love with these immigrants and their first Thanksgiving journey. Lloyd’s extraordinary writing touched my heart and made me laugh out loud – and made me think anew about the idea of America and what it means to so many people.” Tickets ($41 general, $15 college student, $10 high school student) for this production at Aurora Theatre (2081 Addison St., Berkeley) are available online at auroratheatre.org or by phone at 843-4822.

articles.text: Provocative political drama Waste opens February 6 Waste, a provocative Edwardian drama about devious behindthe-scenes political machinations, comes to Marin Theatre in Mill Valley for four weeks opening February 6. Although “Waste” was written in 1906 by the accredited English actor, director and playwright Harley Granville-Barker, a colleague of G.B. Shaw, its public debut was delayed more than 20 years due to outrage over its content. This new production, adapted and directed by Carey Perlof, artistic director emerita of American Conservatory Theater in San Francisco, is a fresh take on the century-old play that shines a spotlight on the issue of reproductive rights. The play follows an ambitious politician on the cusp of bringing his life’s work to fruition. The flawed Henry Trebell, played by Marin Theatre Artistic Director Lance Gardner, finds his promising career curtailed by the threat of scandal over an illicit affair which has led to dire consequences for his wife. Rather than showing sympathy, outrage or even condemnation for the women, the play cynically focuses on the insiders who scheme to use the scandal to manipulate a political outcome. “I am very excited that our audiences will get to experience this remarkable play in my first season as artistic director at Marin Theatre,” said Gardner. “I look forward to returning to the stage, and collaborating with Carey Perloff who returns to direct in the Bay Area for the first time since her tenure at A.C.T.” Waste opened in 1906 in London but was swiftly censored due to its controversial subject matter and critique of societal norms. Finally presented publicly in 1936, Waste earned critical acclaim for its sharp-witted commentary and compelling drama, hailed by The Times as “A masterpiece of its time.” Nearly 100 years later Waste was revived Off-Broadway in 2000. Director Carey Perloff is no stranger to the work of Harley Granville-Barker, given Perloff’s acclaimed production of the playwright’s similarly prescient work about business ethics, The Voysey Inheritance, which was later adapted by David Mamet and received the San Francisco Chronicle’s highest rating. Tickets ($30-$85) for the show at Marin Theatre (397 Miller Avenue, Mill Valley) are available online at MarinTheatre.org or by phone at 415-388-5208. Marin Theatre Artistic Director Lance Gardner will star in the provocative political drama Waste at Marin Theatre from February 6 through March 2.
articles.title: Rare century-old play comes to Marin Theatre

Although “Waste” was written in 1906 by the accredited English actor, director and playwright Harley Granville-Barker, a colleague of G.B. Shaw, its public debut was delayed more than 20 years due to outrage over its content. This new production, adapted and directed by Carey Perlof, artistic director emerita of American Conservatory Theater in San Francisco, is a fresh take on the century-old play that shines a spotlight on the issue of reproductive rights. The play follows an ambitious politician on the cusp of bringing his life’s work to fruition. The flawed Henry Trebell, played by Marin Theatre Artistic Director Lance Gardner, finds his promising career curtailed by the threat of scandal over an illicit affair which has led to dire consequences for his wife. Rather than showing sympathy, outrage or even condemnation for the women, the play cynically focuses on the insiders who scheme to use the scandal to manipulate a political outcome. “I am very excited that our audiences will get to experience this remarkable play in my first season as artistic director at Marin Theatre,” said Gardner. “I look forward to returning to the stage, and collaborating with Carey Perloff who returns to direct in the Bay Area for the first time since her tenure at A.C.T.” Waste opened in 1906 in London but was swiftly censored due to its controversial subject matter and critique of societal norms. articles.text: When Ariel Pawlik-Zwiebel takes the stage at the Young People’s Symphony Orchestra (YPSO) Winter Concert on February 8 at First Church Berkeley, it will be more than a celebration of classical music. As a senior at Campolindo High School in Moraga and YPSO’s co-concertmaster, he is one of the winners of YPSO’s annual Concerto Competition. He will perform the first movement of Jean Sibelius’s Violin Concerto in D Minor, a masterpiece of emotional depth and virtuosity. Beyond music, Ariel is a key member of Highlander Robotics, a student-led team based at Piedmont High School that brings together students from multiple schools to design, build, and program competition-ready robots. As a strategist and drive coach, he played a pivotal role in the team’s success at the FIRST Robotics Competition (FRC) World Championship, where they were a division finalist. Just as in an orchestra, success in robotics depends on teamwork, adaptability, and creative problem-solving. His ability to excel in both fields reflects a broad and deep commitment to learning and achievement, as well as the power of collaboration across disciplines. A dedicated soloist and recitalist, Ariel has performed across the Bay Area and beyond, including a recent appearance at the San Francisco International Piano Festival, collaborating with his father, pianist Markus Pawlik. This season, YPSO violinist Ariel Pawlik-Zwiebel he will also perform the Sibelius Violin Concerto as a soloist with the Livermore-Amador Symphony in February and the Prometheus Symphony in May. Julie Kim, YPSO’s first violin coach, highlights Ariel’s extraordinary commitment: “Ariel’s dedication to his craft and his willingness to grow as a musician are truly remarkable. He brings such passion and focus to his playing, and it’s inspiring to see him excel not only in music but in other areas as well.” YPSO’s Winter Concert will include Marine Safari/Whale Watch from the Monterey Suite by YPSO Composer-in-Residence Jeremy Cavaterra’s, and Antonín Dvořák’s Symphony No. 9 in E Minor, “From the New World.” Tickets are $20 for general admission, and students can attend for free by registering at ypsomusic.org/events.

articles.text: Twyla Tharpe troupe to dance with Philip Glass percussion score For the first time in 10 years, Twyla Tharp’s dance company will return to Zellerbach Hall at UC Berkeley for three performances on Friday, February 7 and 8 at 8 p.m. and February 9 at 3 p.m. The program, celebrating Tharp’s six-decade career as one of the most influential and popular American choreographers of her generation, features the West Coast premiere of Slacktide. The performance will be danced to a score by composer Philip Glass which will be performed live by Chicago’s Grammy-winning Third Coast Percussion, featuring flutist Constance Volk. Tharp will also revive “Diabelli,” a signature ensemble work from 1998 inspired by Beethoven’s Diabelli Variations with music performed live by pianist Vladimir Rumyantsev. In close collaboration with Tharp, Third Coast Percussion has arranged Glass’ hypnotic score Aguas da Amazonia which they will perform live on a collection of custom-designed percussion instruments. Volk will join the group performing a series of flute solos she has composed for the arrangement. Slacktide reunites two titans of contemporary performing arts for the first time in nearly 40 years, since Tharp and Glass’ exhilarating 1986 creation In the Upper Room. Tharp’s choreography captures the layered rhythms and propulsive energy of Glass’ iconic music, here reflecting on the crisis of climate change. In Diabelli Tharp’s choreography highlights the intense humanity of Beethoven’s fiendishly challenging composition, bringing out its humor, pathos and tenderness. The technically demanding work asks dancers to shift effortlessly from ballet to jazz and contemporary dance, even incorporating folk dance. Russian-born pianist Rumyantsev joins the dancers as accompanist and sparring partner for this choreographic and musical journey. Tharp is renowned for creating technically precise works that have pushed the boundaries of ballet and contemporary dance. She founded Twyla Tharp Dance in New York City in 1965; in addition to creating dances for her company and for American Ballet Theatre, she has choreographed Tony-winning Broadway shows, Emmy-winning television specials and blockbuster Hollywood films including Amadeus and Ragtime. Chicago-based Third Coast Percussion is the first percussion ensemble ever to win a Grammy award. Celebrating its 20th anniversary this year, the quartet is best known for interpretations of works by John Cage, Steve Reich and Philip Glass. Tickets ($42-$120) for the show at UC Berkeley’s Zellerbach Hall are available online at calperformances.org, by email at tickets@calperformances.org or by phone at 642-9988. articles.text: Ian Cheung is a quiet young man, quiet and unassuming. And profound. He was the violin soloist last weekend for the Prometheus Symphony concert. Let’s set the scene as if it were a baseball game. Ian is dressed in a jacket and a tie as he approaches home plate. He doesn’t take any practice swings. The pitcher winds up and Ian hits a long one to the deepest reaches of centerfield. The announcer screams: “home run!” Ian rounds the bases and takes a bow when he reaches home plate. The announcer says, “We’ve never seen such calmness in any player.” That was the scene last weekend. Ian Cheung’s vehicle was the First Violin Concerto by Prokofiev. I have never seen a soloist so calmly composed. He walked to his position in the midst of the Orchestra, and then, without any warm-up, proceeded with an interpretation of this unique violin concerto that was masterful. Prokofiev’s First Violin Concerto breaks all the rules. It begins and ends quietly and magically. Only in the second movement is there a display of virtuosity. That Ian Cheung was up to every challenge is putting it mildly. The audience responded enthusiastically. Oh, how I wish he had given us a solo encore. Violin soloist Ian Cheung (center), his teacher Chen Zhou, and Eric Hansen (right), conductor of the Prometheus Symphony after a recent memorable concert.

articles.text: Emma Stone and Ryan Gosling in La La Land I admit that I have always possessed a bias against Hollywood musicals. When dialogue abruptly shifts to singing and music from the background to the foreground, I have found it difficult to suspend my disbelief. And so it was with some reluctance that I sat in a darkened theater and waited for La La Land to begin. I admit that even the title gave me pause. When it started, the opening scene, while energetic, seemed a bit retro (I flashed on Grease). I was already growing restless. Young, beautiful people, stuck on an L.A. freeway in bumper to bumper traffic, suddenly leave their cars and start singing while standing on the hoods and roofs of their cars, the song, Another Day of Sunshine. Palm trees dot the horizon, the colors lift off the screen. A perfect day in L.A… But singing? Dancing? And then something completely unexpected and surprising happens. La La Land becomes almost magical, quickly morphing into a creative and seamless story that is incredibly winning. At the risk of sounding hyperbolic, it is magnificent and wonderful, crafted by writer/ director Damien Chazelle, composed by Justin Hurwitz with lyrics by Benji Pasek and Justin Paul. And what lyrics they are. Together they have created an astonishing collaboration that is transformative and delightful, most especially the theme song, a wistful ballad called City of Stars. So I sit here, with my computer, looking at the screen, asking myself how to write sentences that will encourage moviegoers to discover this film and allow themselves to be swept away by the music and the superb performances of Emma Stone as Mia and Ryan Gosling as Sebastian. Both are denizens of L.A., and both possess dreams yet to be fulfilled. His is to use his talent on the piano to play pure jazz in a club of his own. Hers is to audition (which she does time after time, to heartbreaking effect) for a part that will allow her to not only display her deep reservoir of talent but to truly unleash it. Sebastian and Mia meet briefly, then meet again, and, inevitably, they begin a journey that is heartfelt and sad and wonderful, their moments together enriched by songs and thematic music that will echo for days after you leave the theater. There are moments in this film that are breathtaking, they are so original and filled with artistic risk-taking. At its core La La Land is a simple story: boy meets girl, fall in love, and finally sing and dance as the early evening lights of L.A. appear like so many thousands of surreal stars, the horizon still a gauzy red-purple glow as the sun reluctantly sets. Sensational. Don’t hold back. Trust me. This film is far more than an attempt to pay homage to oldtimey Hollywood musicals that were once so ubiquitous. Chazelle has crafted something glorious and he has elicited from Stone and Gosling startlingly good performances – I mean they are really good. Sit back and open your heart and let La La Land charm you and make you smile, sadly, especially at the end. If given a chance you will be enchanted, I promise. La La Land. Directed by Damien Chazelle, Starring Emma Stone, Ryan Gosling, John Legend. 2 hrs., 8 min. Rated PG-13. Released 2016, Now streaming on Prime/Fandango/Apple tv.

articles.text: One of the deep pleasures of movies is seeing one with companions and then chatting about it when the lights come up. That’s just what Piedmont’s Flix Fest, meeting on the second Thursday of each month offers; a great movie in a comfortable setting, and then a lively discussion of it afterward. January’s Flix Fest offering is the international favorite from Italy, the bittersweet comedy/ drama, Cinema Paradiso. Winning the Academy Award for Best Foreign Film in 1989, the film is often credited with reviving Italy’s film industry. Directed by Giuseppe Tornatore, it was filmed in his small hometown in Sicily. Set a few years after World War II, it focuses on eight-year-old Salvatore (Salvatore Cascio), the bright, mischievous son of a war widow. Nicknamed Toto, he discovers a love for movies and spends every free moment at the local movie house, Cinema Paradiso. Although they initially start on tense terms, he forms a friendship with the middle-aged projectionist, Alfredo (Philippe Noiret), who often lets him watch from the projection booth. The boy finds in the images on the screen the perfect escape from life in his war-torn village. When he grows up, he falls in love with a beautiful local girl (Agnese Nano) and takes over as the Paradiso’s projectionist. Alfredo sets out to persuade Salvatore to leave his small town and pursue his passion for filmmaking. Cinema Paradiso received widespread critical acclaim. Making Tornatore internationally known, it’s regarded by many as a classic. The movie is particularly renowned for the ‘kissing scenes’ montage at its end. The critic Roger Ebert gave it four stars out of four. Cinema Paradiso will be screened in Piedmont on Thursday, February 13, at 1:00 p.m. at the Center for the Arts, 801 Magnolia Avenue. Doors will open at 12:45. The event is free and open to anyone over 18 years of age. Participants are invited on a drop-in basis or register at https:// bit.ly/3PJyxkP. Everyone is welcome to bring snacks or lunch. The next offering in the Piedmont series is one of the most honored of American films, On the Waterfront, directed by Elia Kazan and starring Marlon Brando and Eva Marie Saint, with a stirring score by Leonard Bernstein. It will be shown on March 13th. Watch Cinema Paradiso at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Thursday, February 13th at 1:00 p.m.

articles.text: Moana is a family friendly animated feature by Disney. It is a lively Polynesian story about a strong-willed, adventurous girl named Moana (Auli’i Cravalho), 16, the daughter of her tribe’s chief, Tui (Temuera Morrison). Set on the pacific island of Motunui, an emerald paradise, the story begins with Moana, looking toward the horizon, ever curious, wondering what’s beyond, understanding that for years her tribe has been afraid to venture past the reef that surrounds the island. But a strange cloud now hangs over the island. The fish are not as plentiful and the coconuts dry A scene from Disney Animation studios’ Moana and tasteless. Moana’s grandmother, Tala (Rachel House), tells her that the ocean has chosen her to return the island’s goddess, Te Fifi, an idol stolen by the demigod, Maui (Dwayne Johnson), a millennia ago. Late at night, in the pale moonlight, Moana takes a beached canoe, called a camakan, and sets out, beyond the reef, in search of the hulking, overly confident demigod Maui (Dwayne Johnson). Her mission is to break the spell cast over her people. Moana is clearly Disney’s attempt to feature a young woman who does not need to be rescued by a prince, an almost iconic story line. Instead, the studio approaches the character of Moana with a light hand, the inherent feminism subtle but compelling. Moana is independent, courageous and never burdened with an oppressive patriarchy. Actually, it is her destiny to become the eventual chief of her tribe. There is also no love story, no rugged islander waiting to marry her. Moana is simply a story of an empowered teenage girl on a quest. The directors of the film, John Musker and Ron Clemens (The Little Mermaid, Aladdin) consulted with South Pacific locals, regarding their history and folklore. They also cast a wide net in search of the Hawaiian teen Auli’i Cravalho as the voice of Moana. As well, Dwayne Johnson, adding star power, has Samoan heritage. Voicing Moana’s father, chief Tui, is New Zealander Temuera Morrison of Maori background. Know as well that Moana is sprinkled with 10 songs, sung by Moana and Maui (as it turns out, Johnson has a solid voice).The music was written by Lin-Manuel Miranda, who wrote Hamilton. Plus, the animation is rich in tropical colors. Moana. Directed by John Musker and Ron Clemens. Disney Animation studios. articles.text: It was Lunar New Year on Wednesday last week, but there was another reason for the Walking on Wednesdays group to celebrate. As part of the Piedmont Beautification Foundation’s 60th anniversary, the walkers wanted to see the second of three sets of projects that the PBF has supported during its years of service to Piedmont, the Ramona/Ronada Triangle, the Dracena Park tot lot, and Storyteller Bridge. At each location a PBF volunteer would tell the walkers about the project. A big turnout of 49 walkers and a record eight K-9 best friends were on hand. The morning started off with Matt Gerhardt and PBF President Patty Dunlap telling the group about PBF and what they were going to see that morning. They headed off in a long line going down Highland, Moraga, and Estrella Avenues to Ramona Avenue. Molly Ashford, who lives nearby, shared the Ramona/ Ronada Triangle’s history while a video team from KCOM taped her talk. In the early 2010s residents on Ronada and Ramona Avenues thought this corner was a traffic safety hazard for children going to school. The neighbors felt the crosswalk was too wide and traffic coming off Moraga Ave. was dangerously fast. The residents came to the Park Commission and presented their case for the intersection’s improvement. They had raised money and were willing to financially support improvements. The City appreciated their commitment, and PBF campaigned to raise money to develop this triangle park. It was determined that a small park projecting out from 109 Ronada along with a stop sign would slow traffic. Landscaping with drought tolerant plants and handsome masonry were done, and the park’s opening celebration was Arbor Day 2014. This was also the 50th anniversary of PBF. Molly noted the plants have grown and matured beautifully over the last 10 years. This little park is in the middle of a busy street, but it is also a sanctuary. The walkers headed off down Ramona, up a hidden set of stairs to Arroyo Avenue, and down Ricardo Avenue to the foot of Dracena Park. At each location a PBF volunteer would tell the walkers about the project. A big turnout of 49 walkers and a record eight K-9 best friends were on hand. The morning started off with Matt Gerhardt and PBF President Patty Dunlap telling the group about PBF and what they were going to see that morning. They headed off in a long line going down Highland, Moraga, and Estrella Avenues to Ramona Avenue. In the early 2010s residents on Ronada and Ramona Avenues thought this corner was a traffic safety hazard for children going to school. The neighbors felt the crosswalk was too wide and traffic coming off Moraga Ave. was dangerously fast. The residents came to the Park Commission and presented their case for the intersection’s improvement. They had raised money and were willing to financially support improvements. The City appreciated their commitment, and PBF campaigned to raise money to develop this triangle park. It was determined that a small park projecting out from 109 Ronada along with a stop sign would slow traffic. Landscaping with drought tolerant plants and handsome masonry were done, and the park’s opening celebration was Arbor Day 2014. This was also the 50th anniversary of PBF. Molly noted the plants have grown and matured beautifully over the last 10 years. This little park is in the middle of a busy street, but it is also a sanctuary. articles.text: Beginning in 1974 and culminating in 2011 two major projects have made the Japanese Tea House a beloved part of Piedmont Park, serving as a focal point for weddings and other celebrations. Notably, the Tea House is located on the same site where Frank C. Havens originally built another tea house in 1907. Piedmont Historical Society President Gail Lombardi describes the first chapter in the story succinctly: “The construction of the new Junior High School called for the demolition of the Leander Redman estate next door. The estate was built in 1906 and had a Japanese tea house in the garden. The Board of Education offered the tea house to the City, and in 1974 the tea house was pulled onto a trailer, (and) moved to Piedmont The idea to acquire, relocate and restore the tea house came from the Piedmont Beautification Foundation and the Piedmont Garden Club. Both organizations made it their Bicentennial Project. Community leaders Jean Brown Wolfe, Marnie Winsor and Norma Wells helped make the idea a reality. Wolfe, President of the Garden Club and who had already served as Chair of the Park Commission and President of PBF, convinced the City Council to accept the School District’s offer of the tea house. Through PBF, funds were raised to cover the cost of moving the tea house, preparing the site to receive it, and restoring it to its original condition. To complete the first project, in 1976 a Japanese architect was engaged to design the circular dry rock pond, construct the first decking and complete the landscaping. Installation of the dry rock pond was almost as difficult logistically as moving the building but was ultimately accomplished by Rigging International thanks to Piedmont resident and Rigging President Denny McLeod. On June 27, 1976, City leaders were invited to a Japanese style tea ceremony hosted by Wells and Wolfe to celebrate the completion of Piedmont’s own Japanese Tea House and garden. PBFs continued support showing signs of wear and tear. Both the decking and the Tea House needed repair, and some of the landscaping had deteriorated. At that time, former Mayor Valerie Matzger was President of PBF, and she launched a campaign to restore the Tea House and replace the decking and surrounding garden. In addition to the current decking that anchors the Tea House, several lovely benches were offered as tributary opportunities, providing a significant portion of the funding for the project. Contributions from many Piedmont families The Japanese Tea House today Photo courtesy of Scott Fitzgerrell Photo of the Leander Redman Tea House en route to Piedmont Park The tea house in the gardens of the Redman Estate, pre-1974 were recognized with a brass plaque near the entrance to the garden. At the impetus of Mayor Matzger, and following a unanimous vote of the City Council, the name “Jean Brown Wolfe Tea Garden” is inscribed at the top of the plaque to honor her more than 50 years of service to the City. Wolfe had passed away in February of 2010. On September 27, 2011, the newly restored Tea House and the Jean Brown Wolfe Tea Garden were formally dedicated. PBF President Valerie Matzger emceed the celebration, with a diverse crowd in attendance, including Vice Mayor John Chang, Council member Margaret Fujioka, Public Works Director Chester Nakahara and Japanese Consul General Hiroshi Inomata and his wife Midori. Consul Inomata spoke to the crowd and congratulated the City on the authenticity of the Tea House and Garden. Many members of Wolfe’s family were in attendance, including her son Cameron who stated that “the volunteerism of its citizens is the key to the wonderful character of Piedmont.” Matzger and Wolfe continue to be valued advisors to PBF to this day. PBF further enhances Piedmont Park The Tea House and Tea Garden are not the only PBF projects near the Community Hall. The circular planting bed and Magnolia Tree are among PBF’s earliest projects having been completed in 1967. Landscaping and planting along Cherry Tree Walk soon followed in 1971. PBF recently finished fundraising for the Highland - Guildford Steps and Handrails at Cherry Tree Walk, a project made possible by a generous gift in memory of Denny McLeod made by his wife Ruthie McLeod and their family. McLeod was a past President of the Piedmont Garden Club and served as an Advisor to PBF. Perhaps PBF’s most beloved and long-standing gift to the City is the annual Holiday Tree Lighting, which was first established in 1969 and has since become a cherished tradition in Piedmont. This celebration has recently been expanded to include other winter holidays as “Lights Up Piedmont”. Special thanks to Sharon Hom and Gail Lombardi, whose historical research was instrumental in the creation of this article.

The historic sulfur springs grotto became dilapidated since being built in the 1890s by Frank C. Havens. Designer Mark Feldkamp utilized the remains of the grotto and created a plaza seating area alongside Bushy Dell Creek and connects the grotto to a fern garden and the rest of Piedmont Park. In Piedmont’s infancy Walter Blair capitalized on the springs by bottling the mineral water and erecting a decorative gazebo over the spring for those passing by. articles.text: One of three new mountain lion cubs found in San Mateo County, are now temporarily at Oakland Zoo. On Sunday, January 26, the California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW) brought three orphaned mountain lion cubs to Oakland Zoo for rehabilitation and care. This marks the 30th mountain lion rescue for the Zoo through its close collaboration with CDFW. Oakland Zoo’s advanced Veterinary Hospital has enabled the Zoo to assist in numerous mountain lion rescue cases for those who were sick, injured, burned, or orphaned. The three mountain lion cubs, now named Fern (female), Thistle (male), and Spruce (male), are currently recovering at the Zoo’s Veterinary Hospital. They were found in Portola Valley, San Mateo County. In January, Portola Valley residents spotted the kittens wandering in the neighborhood, and the cubs were later found hiding under a car. CDFW looked for the kittens’ mother for two weeks, using trail cameras and reports from the Midpeninsula Open Space District. There have been no confirmed sightings of an adult female searching or calling for her cubs. Due to their disoriented behavior, lack of a mother for two weeks, and proximity to where an adult female was hit by a vehicle, CDFW decided to capture the kittens for evaluation with help from the Open Space District. Oakland Zoo’s Veterinary Hospital staff conducted a thorough health examination on the three cubs, now named Fern, Thistle, and Spruce, including treatments and bloodwork. The Two of the three mountain lion siblings were transported to Oakland Zoo on January 26. cubs arrived at Oakland Zoo relatively healthy but thin after being without a mother and not receiving adult care for a fortnight. Zoo veterinarians have estimated them to be approximately three months old. Mountain lions in California face many threats, including car strikes and wildfires. These factors contribute to human-wildlife conflict, increasing encounters as mountain lions encroach on urban areas and developments. “As human development has significantly enhanced the wellbeing of our communities, it has simultaneously taken a toll on wildlife and their natural habitats. As we continue to thrive as a species, it is essential for coexistence that we also take action to ensure the survival of others,” said Nik Dehejia, CEO of Oakland Zoo. “We must continually advocate for establishing wildlife corridors, such as the recent overpass in Los Angeles, to maintain the biodiversity of our Golden State.” To support Oakland Zoo’s efforts to rescue and rehabilitate animals in need, please donate at oaklandzoo.org/give An Oakland Zoo veterinarian examining the three cubs on arrival to Oakland Zoo’s Veterinary Hospital. After dinner, something interesting was happening with people’s snacks. Out of view, a gang of mischievous raccoons were plotting a heist of a colorful Cotopaxi backpack that apparently caught their eyes. They started by sending out two goons near the dumpsters across the road. The raccoons made their movements clear, rustling in the bushes and edging as close as possible to human territory. It was only a matter of time before a young Scout spotted their activity. Our forces quickly assembled to yell and bang on pots and sticks to prevent the two raccoons from infiltrating and causing havoc. Little did we know that the rest of the raccoon forces were laughing at us from a safe location 80 meters away. Some Scouts fell for such an elementary decoy. With things going their way, the raccoons finally retrieved a bag with snacks, scampering into the bushes to open their stolen food. But unluckily for them, our young Scout came to the realization that the raccoons stole the bag in a flash. The Scouts organized a hunt and found the bag of food in the bushes. The only signs of the raccoons after that eventful evening were dozens of pairs of beady illuminated eyes from across the road. Troop 15 outsmarted the raccoons this time, but we will surely encounter more wildlife in the future.
